text_blocks.snippet: The Indian Civil Rights Act of 1968 (ICRA) extended certain provisions of the U.S. Bill of Rights to individuals within tribal governments, aiming to protect them from abuses of power. It essentially granted Native Americans living under tribal jurisdiction similar, though not identical, protections to those guaranteed by the Constitution.
snippet_highlighted_words: extended certain provisions of the U.S. Bill of Rights to individuals within tribal governments, aiming to protect them from abuses of power

text_blocks.snippet: Key aspects of the ICRA include:

list.title: Protection of individual rights:
list.snippet: The ICRA ensures that tribal governments cannot infringe upon fundamental rights like freedom of speech, religion, and due process.

list.title: Limitations on tribal government power:
list.snippet: It places limits on tribal governments' authority, preventing them from engaging in actions such as unreasonable search and seizure or taking private property without just compensation.

list.title: Controversy and debate:
list.snippet: The act has been a source of ongoing debate, with some viewing it as an essential protection for individual liberties, while others see it as an infringement on tribal sovereignty and self-governance.

list.title: Enforcement and legal challenges:
list.snippet: The ICRA also provides for federal court enforcement of these rights and has been the subject of numerous legal challenges regarding tribal authority and individual rights.

list.title: Not a complete adoption of the Bill of Rights:
list.snippet: It's crucial to note that the ICRA does not fully mirror the Bill of Rights. For example, while it includes the right to counsel, it does not guarantee free legal counsel in all criminal cases.
